d: Latency numbers every programmer should know, and the five lessons in them
winTitle: You can feel a nanosecond now
goal: Your win today: you can rank memory, disk, data-center and cross-ocean costs from memory, quote the rough numbers (100 ns, 10 ms, 0.5 ms, 150 ms), and use them to justify a cache, batching, or compression.
bookSections: 'Latency numbers every programmer should know' (Table 2-2, Figure 2-1 visualization, and the five conclusions)

stages.title: Order the universe
stages.sub: Sort 13 operations from fastest to slowest
stages.teaches: Units: ns = nanosecond = 10^-9 s; µs = microsecond = 10^-6 s = 1,000 ns; ms = millisecond = 10^-3 s = 1,000 µs. Table 2-2 (Jeff Dean's numbers, roughly 2010-era hardware): L1 cache reference 0.5 ns; branch mispredict 5 ns; L2 cache reference 7 ns; mutex lock/unlock 100 ns; main memory reference 100 ns; compress 1 KB with Zippy (Google's fast compressor, open-sourced as Snappy) 10 µs; send 2 KB over a 1 Gbps network 20 µs; read 1 MB sequentially from memory 250 µs; round trip within the same data center 500 µs; disk seek 10 ms; read 1 MB sequentially from the network 10 ms; read 1 MB sequentially from disk 30 ms; send a packet California → Netherlands → California 150 ms.
stages.interaction: Sort/order mechanic: 13 operation cards shuffled in a column (each card has an icon: CPU chip, RAM stick, spinning disk, network, globe). Learner taps cards in order from fastest to slowest; each tapped card slides into a numbered 'ladder' on the right. Ties (mutex = main memory = 100 ns; disk seek = 1 MB from network = 10 ms) accept either order. After all are placed, the cards reveal their times and re-arrange onto a horizontal log-scale bar chart (each gridline = ×10, from 0.1 ns to 1 s), with misplaced cards outlined in amber and an arrow showing where they belong. Score shows 'X of 13 in the right spot' (counting ties as correct).
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Which is slower: one disk seek, or a round trip to another server in the same data center?' options: 'The disk seek: 10 ms vs 0.5 ms, about 20× slower' (correct) / 'The data-center round trip, because networks are slow' / 'They take about the same time'.

stages.title: If an L1 hit took one second
stages.sub: Stretch time until your gut understands it
stages.teaches: Humans can't feel nanoseconds, so stretch everything by the same factor (×2 billion makes 0.5 ns = 1 s). Then: main memory 100 ns ≈ 3.3 minutes; compress 1 KB ≈ 5.6 hours; data-center round trip 500 µs ≈ 11.6 days; disk seek 10 ms ≈ 7.6 months; read 1 MB from disk 30 ms ≈ 1.9 years; California→Netherlands→California 150 ms ≈ 9.5 years. The gaps are what matter: memory vs disk seek is 100,000×; in-DC vs cross-ocean is 300×. (This human-scale framing is a popular teaching device, not from the book.)
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch. Prompt: 'If an L1 cache hit took 1 second, a disk seek would take about…' options: 'a minute' / 'a day' / 'about 8 months' / 'a century'. After the pick, a vertical timeline zooms out: a clock icon at 1 s, then a 'go make coffee' marker at 3.3 min (memory), a 'sleep on it' marker at 5.6 h (compress), a calendar at 11.6 days (DC round trip), a season change at 7.6 months (disk seek), and finally a '9.5 years' marker (cross-ocean) as the camera keeps zooming out. A toggle switches between 'real time' and 'human time' labels for every operation in the table.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: about 8 months). Then Q.quiz: 'Roughly how many main-memory reads fit in one disk seek?' options: '100,000' (correct: 10 ms ÷ 100 ns) / '100' / '10 million'.

stages.title: Five lessons, four duels
stages.sub: The book's conclusions, proven with a stopwatch
stages.teaches: The book's conclusions from the table: (1) memory is fast but disk is slow; (2) avoid disk seeks if possible; (3) simple compression algorithms are fast; (4) compress data before sending it over the internet if possible; (5) data centers are usually in different regions, and sending data between them takes time. What this means in design: keep hot data in memory (caches), read sequentially rather than seeking randomly, batch calls that cross regions, and shrink bytes before they cross slow, metered links.
stages.interaction: Four head-to-head duels. Each shows two request paths built from operation blocks from the table; the learner predicts which finishes first and roughly by how much (×2 / ×10 / ×100+), then taps 'Race' and two progress bars animate on a time axis (scaled), with totals. Duel 1: read a 1 MB profile blob from memory (250 µs) vs disk seek + 1 MB disk read (10 ms + 30 ms = 40 ms) → memory wins by ~160×. Duel 2: 100 random disk seeks for 100 small records (100 × 10 ms = 1 s) vs one sequential 1 MB read holding all of them (30 ms) → sequential ~33× faster. Duel 3: 5 sequential calls to a service in another region (5 × 150 ms = 750 ms) vs 1 batched call (150 ms) vs 5 calls to a service in the same DC (5 × 0.5 ms = 2.5 ms). Duel 4: compress a 100 KB response (100 × 10 µs = 1 ms) before a cross-ocean trip vs sending it raw; the bar shows the 1 ms compression as a sliver next to the 150 ms round trip, with a note that the real win is fewer bytes on a slow, metered link. After each duel, the matching book conclusion card flips over.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Your API calls a user service in another continent 8 times, one after another, per page load. What's the cheapest big win?' options: 'Batch the calls or keep a copy of the data in the same region' (correct) / 'Buy faster CPUs for the API servers' / 'Switch from L2 to L1 cache on the API boxes'.

stages.title: Old numbers, new hardware
stages.sub: What has changed since 2010, and what never will
stages.teaches: The table is from around 2010. CPU caches and RAM latency have barely moved since. Disks changed most: SSDs (solid-state drives) have no moving head, so a random read costs tens of microseconds instead of a 10 ms seek; sequential reads on NVMe SSDs run at gigabytes per second. Networks went from 1 Gbps to 10–100 Gbps inside data centers. What can't improve is the speed of light: light in fiber travels at about 200,000 km/s, so California↔Netherlands (about 9,000 km by great circle, longer by cable) has a physical round-trip floor of ~90 ms; real routes give ~140–150 ms. Colin Scott's interactive page (book reference [3]) shows the numbers by year (later years are extrapolated, not measured). Interview takeaway: quote the book numbers, then add 'SSDs shrink the disk gap, but cross-region latency is physics'.
stages.interaction: A 'then vs now' toggle over the log-scale chart from stage 1: flipping to 'today (approx.)' slides the disk bars far left (spinning-disk seek 10 ms → SSD random read ~0.1 ms or less, 1 MB sequential from SSD ~1 ms or less) and the network bars a bit left, while memory, in-DC round trip and the California↔Netherlands bar barely move. A 'speed of light' button draws a fiber line on a mini world map between California and the Netherlands and computes 9,000 km ÷ 200,000 km/s = 45 ms one way → 90 ms round-trip floor. Label clearly: 'today values are rough ranges, not a benchmark'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Which number in the table will never get much better with new hardware?' options: 'The cross-ocean round trip; it's bounded by the speed of light' (correct) / 'Disk seek time' / 'Network bandwidth inside a data center'.

stages.title: Boss: The Slow-Request Hydra
stages.sub: Find the head that's eating the latency
stages.teaches: Applies the table: identify the dominant cost in a request path.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '💾 Disk seeks', '🌍 Cross-region round trips', '📦 Too many bytes on the wire', '✅ Fine: memory / same DC'. Scenarios: (1) 'Each feed request does 200 random reads on a spinning disk' → Disk seeks (200 × 10 ms = 2 s); (2) 'A checkout page in Frankfurt calls a pricing service in Oregon 6 times in a row' → Cross-region (~6 × 150 ms ≈ 0.9 s); (3) 'Session lookups hit an in-memory cache in the same data center' → Fine (~0.5 ms round trip); (4) 'The API ships 8 MB of uncompressed JSON to phones on another continent' → Too many bytes (compress; simple compression is cheap); (5) 'A nightly job loads 1 GB by reading row IDs in random order from disk' → Disk seeks (read sequentially instead); (6) 'Rate-limit counters live in RAM on the same box' → Fine (100 ns memory reads).
stages.check: Boss HP; each answer's 'why' shows the arithmetic from Table 2-2.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Recall: use the latency numbers to defend a design choice.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Interviewer: why would you put a cache in front of the database? Use numbers.' Model answer: 'A memory reference is about 100 ns and reading 1 MB from memory about 250 µs, while a disk seek is about 10 ms and reading 1 MB from disk about 30 ms, so memory is roughly 100× faster for bulk reads and 100,000× for random access. A cache in the same data center costs a ~0.5 ms round trip, which is still far cheaper than going to disk. I'd also keep calls inside one region, because a cross-ocean round trip is ~150 ms and that's physics. Caveat: these are 2010-era numbers; SSDs shrink the disk gap, but memory is still much faster.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Quoted memory ~100 ns vs disk seek ~10 ms', 'Mentioned the in-DC round trip (~0.5 ms)', 'Mentioned cross-region ~150 ms', 'Noted SSDs changed the disk numbers'.

caveats: Table 2-2 reflects roughly 2010 hardware. Versions of the list differ slightly (Jeff Dean's slides give mutex lock/unlock as 25 ns and some versions give 20 ms for reading 1 MB from disk); the book uses 100 ns and 30 ms. Treat every number as an order of magnitude.
The 10 ms 'disk seek' is a spinning hard drive. SSD random reads take tens of microseconds, so 'avoid disk seeks' is less dramatic today, but memory is still much faster than any disk.
Colin Scott's interactive chart extrapolates later years from trends; it is not a measured benchmark.
Compression's real win across the internet is fewer bytes on slow or metered links; inside a data center, compressing can cost more CPU time than it saves.
The human-scale 'if L1 were one second' framing is a teaching device, not from the book.
